title: Providence (CCC 302–308)
hook: God guides creation, and invites us to cooperate

segments.voice: Yesterday, almighty: a power the Catechism says shows itself most in mercy. Your line was power as mercy. Where did you choose the gentle strength? Today, how that power guides. Day one thousand seventy.

"Behold the birds of the air, for they neither sow, nor do they reap, nor gather into barns: and your heavenly Father feedeth them." Jesus says it on a hillside, in the Sermon on the Mount, in the Douay-Rheims. It's a lovely line. It also raises a fair question from anyone with a job and a rent payment due on the first. So should we stop sowing? Today's word is the Catechism's way of fitting God's care and our work together: providence.
screen: `THE BIRDS NEITHER SOW NOR REAP.` → `A RENT PAYMENT DUE.` → `SHOULD WE STOP SOWING?`

segments.voice: The Catechism starts somewhere surprising. Creation, it says, wasn't made finished. It was made on a journey, heading toward a fullness it hasn't reached yet. Providence is its name for the ways God guides creation along that road. Scripture, it says, shows that care as concrete and close, reaching the smallest things. That's why Jesus asks for a child's kind of trust: "Seek ye therefore first the kingdom of God, and his justice, and all these things shall be added unto you." Then comes the turn. In the Catholic picture, God isn't a puppeteer. The Catechism says God gives his creatures not only their existence but the dignity of acting on their own, of being real causes for each other. And to human beings he gives the power to share in providence freely: to tend the earth, to work, to look after one another. Paul has a word for it. Writing about himself and the others who labored with him in Corinth, he says, in the Douay-Rheims, "we are God's coadjutors." Coadjutors: helpers, fellow workers. The Catechism takes up that phrase for people more broadly. It says that through their actions, their prayers, and even their sufferings, people can enter freely into God's plan, and so become God's fellow workers. So, back to the birds. They don't sow. People do. And on this reading, the sowing itself can be part of how God provides. Providence isn't a reason to sit still, and it isn't a promise that nothing will go wrong. It's trust that God is at work, and an invitation to work alongside. That's the carry: we are co-workers.
screen: `CREATION MADE ON A JOURNEY.` · `SEEK FIRST THE KINGDOM.` · `NOT A PUPPETEER: REAL CAUSES.` · `WE ARE GOD'S COADJUTORS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trust one detail to God, or, if that's not your language, set one worry down. Settle, and breathe. Pick one thing you're carrying this week, small or not so small: a bill, a test result, a hard conversation. Hold it up in your mind. Ask two questions. What part of this is mine to do? And what part is out of my hands? Name your part: one step, nothing more. Then let the other part go, for now. If you pray, you can hand that part to God in your own words. If you don't, practice setting it down for as long as the bell rings. The bell holds the time.
Providence. God's guidance of a creation still on its way, and the invitation to share in that work freely. Today's word.
Your line: we are co-workers. Today, take the one step you named, and leave the rest where you set it down. Day one thousand seventy.

howItsDone: Catholics speak of trusting in divine providence, and pair that trust with work; some pray before a task or a decision and offer the day's work to God in a morning prayer.

fork.setup: rent is due, and you've just heard the line about the birds who neither sow nor reap. what does the Catechism's reading point to?
options: work, and trust God in the work
worry, since it all depends on you
fork.reveal: the Catechism says God invites people to share in providence through their actions, prayers and sufferings, as God's fellow workers.

original.note: Greek: providence. The word in Wisdom 14:3 for the Father's providence.

trapdoor: what you thought: providence means everything is already scripted.
what it means: God guides a creation still on its way, and gives creatures the dignity of real action, inviting people to cooperate.
what a scholar hears: CCC 302's creation 'in a state of journeying', CCC 306–307 on creatures as real causes and people as God's fellow workers, and 1 Corinthians 3:9's 'coadjutors'.

notes: Confirm Challoner wording of Matthew 6:26, 6:33 and 1 Corinthians 3:9 ('For we are God's coadjutors').

Catechism paraphrased (copyright): creation 'in a state of journeying' (CCC 302); concrete and immediate care (CCC 303); childlike abandonment, citing Matthew 6:31–33 (CCC 305); the dignity of being causes (CCC 306); sharing in providence through actions, prayers and sufferings, as God's fellow workers (CCC 307). Confirm.
1 Corinthians 3:9: Paul is speaking of himself and Apollos; the script says so, and says the Catechism applies the phrase more broadly.
Hook: 'due on the first' is illustrative, not a claim.
Original: πρόνοια glossed 'forethought'; this is a lexicon sense not stated in the day's cited text. Its use in Greek Wisdom 14:3 ('thy providence, O Father') to be confirmed. Keeper may set to null.
